group: PSI Score: Pneumonia Severity Index for CAP
question:
Patient note:
A 26-year-old woman who works as an elementary-school art teacher and shares a basement apartment with two roommates presented to the emergency department in the early afternoon after waking with a second night of shaking chills, pleuritic left-sided chest discomfort, and an incessant dry cough that turned scantily productive only this morning; she measured an oral temperature of 38 °C at home, declined the acetaminophen her roommate offered, and rode a rideshare the ten city blocks to the hospital so the clinical team could record an unaltered physiologic profile. Her medical history is notable for stage IIB Hodgkin lymphoma treated with ABVD chemotherapy four years ago, followed by a consolidative involved-field radiation course; she has remained in complete remission on annual surveillance, takes no chronic medications beyond a daily vitamin, and has no record of kidney impairment, cerebrovascular insult, chronic liver disorder, or cardiomyopathy. She never smoked, drinks a single cider on rare weekends, and denies recreational drug use. Immunization records in the state registry confirm receipt of both pneumococcal formulations and this season’s inactivated influenza vaccine. On arrival she sat bolt upright on the stretcher, conversing in full sentences, maintaining eye contact, and correctly stating the date, location, and current national holiday, without agitation or confusion. Untreated triage vital signs while breathing ambient air at this sea-level facility measured: oral temperature 38.05 °C, an impressively rapid and regular radial pulse of 147 beats per minute corroborated on a three-lead monitor as sinus tachycardia without ectopy, automated blood pressure 123/71 mm Hg verified manually, respirations counted for a full minute at 62 breaths per minute with shallow excursions and visible alar flaring, and fingertip pulse oximetry fluctuating between 96 % and 97 %. Skin was warm and lightly diaphoretic but capillary refill remained brisk; conjunctivae appeared ruddy, and there was no digital clubbing or peripheral edema. Jugular venous pulsation did not rise above the sternal angle at 45°, and heart sounds revealed a forceful S1/S2 without murmurs, gallops, or rubs. Pulmonary examination disclosed coarse crackles over the left mid-axillary and posterior lower fields with preserved resonance to percussion; the right lung transmitted vesicular breath sounds throughout, and no dull stony note suggesting free fluid was elicited in either costophrenic recess. The abdomen was flat and nontender with normal bowel sounds and no organomegaly. A focused neurologic screen showed equal, reactive pupils, intact extra-ocular movements, 5/5 symmetric strength, and a normal finger-to-nose test. Capillary glucose obtained before vascular access read 158 mg/dL. Venous blood drawn within ten minutes of bay entry—prior to any crystalloid bolus, antibiotics, or heparinized saline larger than the 3 mL used to lock the catheter—revealed sodium 108 mEq/L, potassium 3.7 mEq/L, chloride 79 mEq/L, bicarbonate 20 mEq/L, blood urea nitrogen 16 mg/dL, and creatinine 0.7 mg/dL. Complete blood count demonstrated leukocytes 13.4 × 10⁹/L with 86 % segmented neutrophils, hematocrit a striking 67 %, hemoglobin 22.1 g/dL, and platelet count 235 × 10⁹/L. A right radial arterial sample obtained as she remained on room air showed pH 7.74, PaCO₂ 19 mm Hg, PaO₂ 108 mm Hg, and calculated bicarbonate 20 mEq/L, consistent with a primary respiratory alkalosis driven by her profound tachypnea. Serum lactate measured 1.9 mmol/L, and high-sensitivity troponin fell below the assay threshold. Portable postero-anterior and lateral chest radiographs acquired fifteen minutes into the encounter—well before any antimicrobials, corticosteroids, bronchodilators, or supplemental oxygen—demonstrated a patchy consolidation in the lingular segment of the left upper lobe extending toward the inferior hilum without costophrenic angle blunting, layering opacity, or meniscus sign, and with a cardiac silhouette of normal size. Electrocardiography displayed sinus tachycardia at 146 beats per minute with nonspecific ST-T wave changes but no acute ischemic pattern. Two sets of peripheral blood cultures, a nurse-assisted expectorated sputum sample for Gram stain and culture, urinary antigens for Streptococcus pneumoniae and Legionella pneumophila, and a multiplex respiratory viral PCR panel were dispatched to the laboratory before any empiric therapy was initiated. Up to the moment this narrative is filed she has received no intravenous fluids, antipyretics, vasopressors, bronchodilators, corticosteroids, or supplemental oxygen, ensuring that every vital sign, laboratory value, and imaging finding above reflects her untreated presentation.

Question: What is the patient's Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI)? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI) adds demographic, comorbidity, examination, and test-result points from the untreated presentation.
- Demographics: age 26 minus 10 for female sex = 16. She lives at home, so nursing-home residence adds 0.
- Examination: respiratory rate 62/min (≥30) adds 20; pulse 147/min (≥125) adds 10. Normal mentation, systolic pressure 123 mm Hg (≥90), and temperature 38.05 °C (neither <35 nor ≥40) add 0.
- Tests: sodium 108 mEq/L (<130) adds 20. Arterial pH 7.74 is not <7.35, BUN 16 is not ≥30 mg/dL, glucose 158 is not ≥250 mg/dL, hematocrit 67% is not <30%, and PaO₂ 108 is not <60 mm Hg. None adds points. No pleural effusion: 0.
- Comorbidities: no liver, heart, cerebrovascular, or renal disease adds points. The result depends on how the lymphoma is coded. The standard PSI counts active cancer or cancer diagnosed within the preceding year; four years in remission does not qualify, giving 16 + 20 + 10 + 20 = 66. If lymphoma history is counted as neoplastic disease (+30) regardless of remission, the conditional total is 66 + 30 = 96.
Final answer: 96
